notes.b: Green plants make their own food. They build glucose, a carbohydrate, from carbon dioxide and water, using light energy, and this process is photosynthesis.
points: Plants are producers because they make their own food. Animals, including people, are consumers: they get their carbohydrate by eating plants, or animals that ate plants.
Word equation: carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of light and chlorophyll, gives glucose + oxygen.
Balanced equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, with light energy and chlorophyll written above the arrow. It is balanced because there are 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side.
Four things are required: light energy, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water. There are two products: glucose and oxygen.
Light energy is changed into chemical energy stored in the glucose molecule. This stored energy is what a person later releases from carbohydrate in respiration.

Chlorophyll is the green pigment (colouring substance) in the chloroplasts, the parts of leaf cells where photosynthesis takes place. It absorbs light energy, mainly red and blue light, and uses it to drive the reaction.
Chlorophyll reflects green light rather than absorbing it, which is why leaves look green.

Diagram: leaf cross-section labelled with stomata, palisade cells containing chloroplasts, xylem and phloem, with arrows showing carbon dioxide entering, oxygen leaving, water entering through the xylem and sucrose leaving through the phloem.
notes.tip: A short answer should give the equation, the four requirements and the two products. The oxygen is a by-product, not a raw material: carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials, and chlorophyll reflects green light rather than absorbing it.

notes.h: Getting the raw materials to the leaf
notes.b: A leaf can only make glucose if carbon dioxide, water and light all reach its cells. Each arrives by its own route, and the oxygen made leaves by one of them.
points: Carbon dioxide enters the leaf from the air by diffusion (spreading from where there is more of it to where there is less) through stomata, small pores mainly on the lower surface of the leaf.
Root hair cells absorb water from the soil, and it is carried up the stem to the leaves in the xylem, the tubes that carry water.
Light comes from the sun.
Oxygen, the by-product of photosynthesis, diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata. Some of it is used by the plant in its own respiration.
Respiration goes on in plant cells all the time, day and night, whereas photosynthesis needs light. This is why plants do not simply breathe in carbon dioxide by day and oxygen by night.
notes.tip: Give the raw materials with their routes in one line: carbon dioxide through the stomata, water through the root hair cells and up the xylem. Plants respire all the time and photosynthesise only in light, so never call photosynthesis the opposite of breathing.

notes.h: What the plant does with its glucose
notes.b: A plant does not keep its glucose as glucose. It uses it for energy, stores it, moves it and builds with it, and each job uses a different form.
points: Respiration: some glucose is used immediately to release energy for growth and the plant's other processes.
Starch: surplus glucose is joined into starch, an insoluble polysaccharide (a large carbohydrate made of many glucose units) kept as a store in leaves, stems, roots and tubers such as potatoes.
Starch is insoluble, so it can be stored in large amounts without affecting the water balance of the cell.

Sucrose: glucose is converted to sucrose, which is carried in the phloem, the transport tubes for sugars, from the leaves to the other parts of the plant, such as growing tips, roots, fruits and storage organs.
Cellulose: glucose is joined into cellulose, the main structural material of plant cell walls.
Plants also make fruit sugars (glucose and fructose), pectin in their cell walls, and, with nitrogen from the soil, proteins, and from glucose, oils and other lipids.
notes.tip: Name the three uses of glucose: respiration, starch for storage and cellulose for cell walls. Give the transport form as sucrose in the phloem. Glucose is not the form in which a plant stores or moves carbohydrate, so never say glucose travels in the phloem.

notes.b: Every carbohydrate in a person's diet starts in a plant. This link is the opening of any answer about where carbohydrates come from.
points: Plants make glucose by photosynthesis and join it into larger carbohydrates, so every sugar, starch and fibre in the diet was first made by a plant.
Plant foods supply carbohydrate directly, and animal foods supply it indirectly because animal feed is plant material.
Lactose in milk is made by the animal from glucose; it is not made by plants.
Fibre in the diet is cellulose, which is plant cell-wall material.
Photosynthesis also releases the oxygen that people use in aerobic respiration (respiration using oxygen).
notes.tip: If asked where carbohydrates come from, say plants make glucose by photosynthesis and join it into larger carbohydrates. Then link starch, sucrose and cellulose to their uses, with fibre as plant cell-wall material.

keyTerms.definition: The process by which green plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.
The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
The organelle in leaf cells that contains chlorophyll and is the site of photosynthesis.
Small pores, mainly on the underside of a leaf, through which carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves.
An organism, such as a green plant, that makes its own food from simple substances.
The plant tissue that carries water and mineral salts up from the roots to the leaves.
The plant tissue that transports sucrose and other dissolved food from the leaves to the rest of the plant.
An insoluble polysaccharide that plants store in leaves, stems, roots and tubers as an energy reserve.

factCards.definition: Light energy, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water.
Glucose, which the plant uses or stores, and oxygen, which is released.

factCards.term: Three things a plant does with surplus glucose
factCards.definition: Converts it to starch for storage, to cellulose for cell walls, or to sucrose for transport.

factCards.term: Two gases exchanged through the stomata
factCards.definition: Carbon dioxide enters the leaf and oxygen leaves it.

factCards.term: Route taken by water in a plant
factCards.definition: From the roots, up the stem to the leaves, through the xylem.

questions.prompt: Explain how a green plant converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose, naming the energy source and the gas released.
questions.model: Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts. Carbon dioxide enters the leaf through the stomata and water is absorbed by the roots and carried to the leaves in the xylem. The reaction produces glucose, and oxygen is released as a by-product through the stomata.

questions.prompt: Trace the route of carbohydrate from its formation in a leaf to its storage and use within the plant, and explain why photosynthesis matters to people.
questions.model: Glucose is formed in the chloroplasts of leaf cells by photosynthesis. The plant uses some glucose in respiration to release energy for growth. Surplus glucose is joined into starch and stored in leaves, stems, roots and tubers. Glucose is converted to sucrose and transported in the phloem to other parts of the plant. Glucose is also joined into cellulose to build cell walls. People depend on photosynthesis because plants are producers: all dietary carbohydrate comes directly from plants or from animals that eat plants. Photosynthesis also releases the oxygen needed for aerobic respiration.
